content: Vaginal discharge is a frequent concern among patients, often accompanied by anxiety about sexually transmitted diseases (STDs). If an STD is identified, it is essential to screen for other potential STDs. Patients diagnosed with an STD should be advised to inform all sexual partners about their condition. It is also important to note that vaginal discharge can be a normal physiological occurrence, influenced by periodic hormonal changes. Vaginal discharge is a combination of fluid, cells, and bacteria that serves to lubricate and protect the vaginal environment. It is produced by the cells of the vagina and cervix. The characteristics of normal vaginal discharge vary throughout the menstrual cycle. For example, during ovulation, the discharge is typically clear and stretchable, while in the luteal phase, it may become thicker and slightly yellow. Healthy vaginal discharge should not be associated with symptoms such as itching, redness, swelling, or a strong odor. A thorough medical history should be obtained, including any associated symptoms such as painful urination (dysuria), pain during intercourse (dyspareunia), lower abdominal pain, itching, or fever. When evaluating the causes of vaginal discharge, it is critical to differentiate between infectious and non-infectious etiologies. Infectious causes include pathogens such as Candida albicans, Trichomonas vaginalis, Gardnerella vaginalis, Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and the Herpes Simplex Virus. Diagnosis of these infections should be confirmed through laboratory tests and cultures. Non-infectious causes may include hormonal changes during puberty, the menstrual cycle, the presence of a foreign body, cervical or vaginal cancer, diabetes, or other systemic conditions. Common Causes of Vaginal Discharge: 1. Atrophic Vaginitis (Senile Vaginitis): This condition results from estrogen deficiency, leading to vaginal dryness, itching, irritation, discharge, and painful intercourse. 2. Bacterial Vaginosis: Common in women of reproductive age, this condition is characterized by a shift in vaginal flora from predominantly Lactobacillus to a polymicrobial environment. 3. Cervical Cancer: Vaginal discharge may be a symptom of malignancy. 4. Chlamydia: A sexually transmitted infection that can cause abnormal discharge. 5. Foreign Body Vaginitis: Retained foreign objects in the vagina can lead to irritation and discharge. 6. Gonorrhea: A sexually transmitted infection that may present with discharge. 7. Herpes Simplex Virus: This viral infection can cause lesions and discharge. 8. Trichomoniasis: A parasitic infection typically transmitted through unprotected sexual contact. 9. Vaginal Cancer: Malignancy of the vaginal tissue can result in abnormal discharge. 10. Vaginal Yeast Infection: Overgrowth of Candida species can lead to thick, white discharge. 11. Diabetes: Poorly controlled diabetes can predispose individuals to infections causing discharge. 12. Drug Side Effects: Certain medications, such as antibiotics, steroids, and hormonal therapies, can alter the vaginal environment and lead to discharge. Classification of Vaginal Discharge: Normal Discharge: Occurs in various life stages, including neonatal, pediatric, puberty, menstrual cycle, pregnancy, and menopause. Abnormal Discharge: Includes conditions such as bacterial vaginosis, yeast infections, STDs, vaginal cancer, and cervical cancer. Laboratory Investigations: Initial diagnostic tests should include: Complete Blood Count (CBC) Urinalysis Urine culture Beta-hCG (to rule out pregnancy) Gonorrhea culture Chlamydia culture Referral to a Gynecologist: Patients should be referred to a specialist if they present with: Retained foreign bodies Recent surgical or procedural interventions involving the genital tract Suspected genital tract tumors Cervical ectopy or polyps Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis Abnormal discharge during pregnancy Symptoms of upper genital tract infections, such as fever and lower abdominal pain Treatment During Pregnancy: 1. Vulvovaginal Candidiasis: Topical azole therapies for 7 days are recommended. 2. Trichomoniasis: A single oral dose of 2 g metronidazole is recommended. Symptomatic pregnant women should be tested and treated regardless of the stage of pregnancy. 3. Bacterial Vaginosis: Symptomatic pregnant women should be treated. A 250 mg regimen of metronidazole is effective, but 500 mg twice daily can also be used. Acute Pharmacotherapies: 1. Bacterial Vaginosis: Metronidazole, administered as a single dose or over 7 days. 2. Candida and Chlamydia: Azithromycin or doxycycline. 3. Gonorrhea: Oral ciprofloxacin or intramuscular ceftriaxone. 4. Trichomoniasis: Metronidazole, either as a single dose or over 7 days. For pregnant women or those unable to tolerate metronidazole, intravaginal clotrimazole may be used.
